ml_algorithm_reference_sheet.description: A world-class, exhaustive reference sheet of  foundational and modern machine learning algorithms, enriched with ELI5 (Explain Like I'm 5) analogies, metadata, and use-cases.

algorithms.eli5: Making all your toys the same size so they fit perfectly in a box.
algorithms.purpose: Standardizes features to zero mean and unit variance.

algorithms.eli5: Sorting toys by size but ignoring the one giant teddy bear so it doesn't mess up the rest.
algorithms.purpose: Scales data using median and IQR, robust to outliers.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing new pictures of rare animals by mixing the features of the few pictures you already have.
algorithms.purpose: Generates synthetic minority samples via interpolation.

algorithms.eli5: Turning a list of favorite colors into a checklist where only one box is checked per person.
algorithms.purpose: Converts categorical integers into binary vectors.

algorithms.eli5: Squishing a big box of toys into a smaller box by only keeping the most important ones.
algorithms.purpose: Projects data into lower-dimensional subspace capturing max variance.

algorithms.eli5: Taking a big group of people and arranging them on a map so friends stand close together.
algorithms.purpose: Non-linear dim reduction for 2D/3D visualization via KL divergence.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a straight line through dots to guess where the next dot will be.
algorithms.purpose: Models linear relationship minimizing squared residuals.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a line but putting a gentle leash on it so it doesn't go crazy.
algorithms.purpose: L2 penalty shrinks coefficients to handle multicollinearity.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a line and throwing away the markers you don't really need.
algorithms.purpose: L1 penalty induces sparsity for implicit feature selection.

algorithms.eli5: Asking a hundred friends to guess an answer, then picking the most popular guess.
algorithms.purpose: Bagging ensemble of decorrelated decision trees.

algorithms.eli5: A team of students where each one specifically studies the questions the last student got wrong.
algorithms.purpose: Highly optimized gradient tree boosting with regularization.

algorithms.eli5: A super-fast study group that grows the tree downwards first, focusing on the hardest homework problems.
algorithms.purpose: Gradient boosting using leaf-wise tree growth and GOSS.

cons: Prone to overfitting on small data

algorithms.eli5: A smart tutor that naturally understands words and categories without needing you to translate them first.
algorithms.purpose: Gradient boosting with native categorical feature support.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a line in the sand to decide which team a new player belongs to.
algorithms.purpose: Models log-odds of discrete classes using a sigmoid function.

algorithms.eli5: Finding the widest possible street that separates the red houses from the blue houses.
algorithms.purpose: Maximizes margin between classes using support vectors and kernels.

algorithms.eli5: Asking your closest neighbors what they think, and doing what the majority of them do.
algorithms.purpose: Classifies/regresses based on majority vote/average of K closest points.

algorithms.eli5: Guessing it's a dog because it barks, wags its tail, and has fur, assuming each clue is independent.
algorithms.purpose: Applies Bayes' theorem with naive feature independence assumption.

algorithms.eli5: Sorting a pile of mixed candies into bowls based on which ones look most similar.
algorithms.purpose: Partitions data into K clusters by minimizing inertia to centroids.

algorithms.eli5: Finding crowds of people at a party and ignoring the lonely folks standing in the corners.
algorithms.purpose: Density-based clustering identifying arbitrary shapes and noise.

algorithms.eli5: Playing a guessing game where you ask random questions until you isolate the weird kid who doesn't fit in.
algorithms.purpose: Isolates anomalies by randomly partitioning data.

algorithms.eli5: Playing a game of 20 Questions to guess what object you're thinking of.
algorithms.purpose: Hierarchical splitting based on impurity (Gini/Entropy) or variance.

algorithms.eli5: A sculptor who starts with a rough block and makes tiny, precise chisels to fix the mistakes of the last stroke.
algorithms.purpose: Sequential additive ensemble fitting negative gradients of loss.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a line that not only separates red and blue balls, but also squishes them as close to their own team's center as possible.
algorithms.purpose: Maximizes class separability by projecting data onto lower dimensions.

algorithms.eli5: Saying a point belongs 80% to the red team and 20% to the blue team based on overlapping clouds of probability.
algorithms.purpose: Soft clustering using weighted multivariate Gaussians via EM.

algorithms.eli5: Giving every word a GPS coordinate so 'king' and 'queen' are neighbors, and 'dog' is far away.
algorithms.purpose: Maps words to dense vectors capturing semantic similarity.

algorithms.eli5: Highlighting the rare, important words in a book, while ignoring common words like 'the' and 'and'.
algorithms.purpose: Weighs term frequency by inverse document frequency.

algorithms.eli5: Reading a bunch of articles and figuring out that 'sports' articles use words like 'ball' and 'score' a lot.
algorithms.purpose: Generative probabilistic model for discovering hidden topics in text.

algorithms.eli5: Figuring out your favorite movie genres by looking at what you watched, and matching you with others who like the same genres.
algorithms.purpose: Matrix factorization for collaborative filtering via alternating optimization.

algorithms.eli5: A brain made of layers of tiny calculators that pass notes to each other to solve a really hard puzzle.
algorithms.purpose: Feedforward neural network for complex non-linear mappings.

algorithms.eli5: Looking at a photo through a tiny magnifying glass, sliding it across the image to find edges, then shapes, then whole objects.
algorithms.purpose: Processes grid data using convolutional filters for spatial hierarchies.

algorithms.eli5: Reading a book and keeping a mental sticky note of the main characters so you remember who they are by chapter 10.
algorithms.purpose: RNN variant with gating mechanisms to capture long-term dependencies.

algorithms.eli5: Building a super-tall Lego tower, but adding secret skip-doors so you can jump up 10 floors at once without the tower collapsing.
algorithms.purpose: Deep CNN using skip connections to solve vanishing gradients.

algorithms.eli5: Glancing at a messy room and instantly pointing out where the shoes, books, and keys are all at the same time.
algorithms.purpose: Real-time object detection treating detection as a single regression problem.

algorithms.eli5: Tracing a picture, then zooming out to see the whole page, ensuring every single pixel is colored in perfectly.
algorithms.purpose: Encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections for precise pixel-wise segmentation.

algorithms.eli5: An art forger trying to paint a fake Mona Lisa, while a detective tries to catch the fake, until the forgery is perfect.
algorithms.purpose: Generator and Discriminator networks contest to produce realistic synthetic data.

algorithms.eli5: Learning to draw a cat by squishing it into a simple sketch, then using the sketch to draw a brand new, slightly different cat.
algorithms.purpose: Generative model learning latent probability distributions via encoder-decoder.

algorithms.eli5: Starting with a TV screen full of static, and slowly, step-by-step, wiping away the static to reveal a perfect photograph.
algorithms.purpose: Generative model learning to reverse a gradual noising process.

algorithms.eli5: Reading a whole sentence at once, looking at all the words together to understand that 'bank' means a river edge, not money.
algorithms.purpose: Bidirectional transformer for deep contextual word representations.

algorithms.eli5: A super-smart autocomplete that has read the entire internet and can write essays, code, or stories word-by-word.
algorithms.purpose: Autoregressive transformer predicting next token based on previous context.

algorithms.eli5: Teaching a computer to look at a picture of a dog and a sentence 'a fluffy dog' and knowing they mean the exact same thing.
algorithms.purpose: Contrastive learning aligning image and text embeddings in a shared space.

algorithms.eli5: Figuring out what a person is like by looking at their friends, and what their friends are like by looking at their friends.
algorithms.purpose: Aggregates neighbor features in a graph to learn node representations.

algorithms.eli5: A maze runner getting a cookie for right turns and a timeout for wrong turns until it memorizes the perfect path.
algorithms.purpose: Model-free RL finding optimal action-selection policy via Q-values.

algorithms.eli5: Using a brain (neural network) to guess the cookie-value of every possible move in a massive video game.
algorithms.purpose: Q-learning using a deep neural network to approximate Q-values.

algorithms.eli5: Training a dog with treats, but making sure you don't change the rules too drastically between tricks so the dog doesn't get confused.
algorithms.purpose: Policy gradient method restricting step size for stable training.

algorithms.eli5: Predicting next year's ice cream sales by looking at last year's sales, plus knowing summer is hot and December has holidays.
algorithms.purpose: Additive model capturing trend, seasonality, and holidays.

algorithms.eli5: Guessing tomorrow's weather based on today's weather, yesterday's weather, and any sudden shocks that happened.
algorithms.purpose: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average for stationary time-series.

algorithms.eli5: Organizing a massive library of books into neighborhoods where similar books are close, preserving the whole map's layout.
algorithms.purpose: Manifold learning preserving global and local structure via topological data.

algorithms.eli5: Finding the odd one out by asking random yes/no questions until only the weird object is left alone.
algorithms.purpose: Isolates anomalies by randomly partitioning data.

algorithms.eli5: A neural network that learns to read a spreadsheet by choosing which columns to look at first, just like a human expert.
algorithms.purpose: Attentive sequential neural network for tabular data.

algorithms.eli5: Using a brain to learn your hidden tastes and matching you with movies based on deep patterns, not just simple star ratings.
algorithms.purpose: Replaces dot-product of matrix factorization with a deep neural network.

algorithms.eli5: Chopping a picture into tiny puzzle pieces and treating them like words in a sentence to understand the whole image.
algorithms.purpose: Applies standard Transformer architecture directly to sequences of image patches.

algorithms.eli5: Learning that 'unbelievable' is made of 'un', 'believe', and 'able', so it understands new words it has never seen before.
algorithms.purpose: Word embeddings based on character n-grams.

algorithms.eli5: BERT's older, smarter sibling who read the same books but spent 10x longer studying and didn't skip any chapters.
algorithms.purpose: Optimized BERT pre-training removing dynamic masking.

algorithms.eli5: A universal translator that treats every language task—translation, summarization, Q&A—as just translating text into different text.
algorithms.purpose: Unified encoder-decoder framework for all NLP tasks.

algorithms.eli5: Understanding that 'play' means something different in 'play a game' vs 'play a guitar' by reading the whole sentence first.
algorithms.purpose: Contextualized word representations using bidirectional LSTMs.

algorithms.eli5: A universal ear that listens to anyone speaking in any language and instantly types it out perfectly.
algorithms.purpose: Multilingual, multi-task speech recognition via Transformer.

algorithms.eli5: Letting an AI take an open-book test, where it searches a library for facts before writing its answer.
algorithms.purpose: Combines retrieval system with generative LLM to ground outputs.

algorithms.eli5: Instead of rewriting a whole textbook, you just add a few sticky notes with corrections to the pages that matter.
algorithms.purpose: Freezes pre-trained weights and injects trainable low-rank matrices.

cons: Slight performance drop vs full FT

algorithms.eli5: A wise, giant owl teaching a tiny, fast sparrow how to hunt, so the sparrow can do a good job without being huge.
algorithms.purpose: Transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a small student model.

algorithms.eli5: Showing the computer two slightly different photos of the same cat and saying 'these are the same', then a photo of a dog saying 'these are different'.
algorithms.purpose: Learns representations by pulling similar pairs together and pushing dissimilar apart.

algorithms.eli5: Taking a few 2D photos of a statue and using a brain to imagine what it looks like from every possible angle in 3D.
algorithms.purpose: Optimizes a continuous volumetric scene representation using sparse images.

algorithms.eli5: A hundred doctors each studying their own patients' secret files, then just sharing their general notes to write a single medical book, without sharing patient names.
algorithms.purpose: Trains ML models across decentralized devices holding local data.

algorithms.eli5: Figuring out what a person is like, but paying way more attention to their best friends than to their random acquaintances.
algorithms.purpose: Graph neural network using attention mechanisms to weight neighbor importance.

algorithms.eli5: Moving all the marbles on a bumpy table uphill until they all settle into the highest peaks, forming natural groups.
algorithms.purpose: Centroid-based algorithm that assigns datapoints to regions of highest density.

algorithms.eli5: A classroom voting for class representatives, where students pass messages about who they think is best, until a consensus is reached.
algorithms.purpose: Identifies exemplars that best represent the data via message passing.

algorithms.eli5: Connecting dots on a page with rubber bands based on how close they are, then cutting the bands to separate the groups.
algorithms.purpose: Uses eigenvalues of similarity matrix Laplacian for dim reduction before clustering.

algorithms.eli5: Building a family tree of data points, grouping them into tiny sub-families first, then merging the families to save memory.
algorithms.purpose: Incremental hierarchical clustering using a CF-Tree for massive datasets.

algorithms.eli5: Starting with every person as their own island, then building bridges to connect the closest islands until you have a few continents.
algorithms.purpose: Bottom-up hierarchical clustering merging pairs based on linkage.

algorithms.eli5: Rearranging a giant spreadsheet of students and subjects so that blocks of students who like the same subjects form perfect squares.
algorithms.purpose: Simultaneously clusters rows and columns of a matrix.

algorithms.eli5: Taking a complex painting and figuring out exactly which basic tubes of paint (only bright colors, no mixing darks) were used to make it.
algorithms.purpose: Factorizes non-negative matrices into additive, parts-based representations.

algorithms.eli5: Being at a loud party and using your brain to isolate and listen to just one specific friend's voice.
algorithms.purpose: Separates mixed signals into independent non-Gaussian sources.

algorithms.eli5: Learning a secret alphabet of basic shapes so you can draw any picture using only a few quick strokes.
algorithms.purpose: Finds an over-complete dictionary of atoms for sparse data representation.

algorithms.eli5: Lifting a tangled pile of red and blue strings into the air, then slicing through them with a flat plane to separate the colors.
algorithms.purpose: Applies kernel trick to PCA for non-linear dimensionality reduction.

algorithms.eli5: Finding the main themes of a book, but forcing each theme to only be described using a few specific words.
algorithms.purpose: PCA with L1 penalty to extract sparse, interpretable components.

algorithms.eli5: Realizing that 'doctor' and 'hospital' often appear together, so the computer groups them into a hidden 'health' concept.
algorithms.purpose: Applies Truncated SVD to document-term matrices to find latent topics.

algorithms.eli5: Like LSA, but using strict probability math to say 'there is an 80% chance this document is about sports'.
algorithms.purpose: Probabilistic topic model using Expectation-Maximization.

algorithms.eli5: Using a dictionary of happy and sad words, plus rules for exclamation marks and emojis, to guess if a text message is angry or joyful.
algorithms.purpose: Lexicon and rule-based sentiment analysis tuned for social media.

algorithms.eli5: Finding a group of people who have the exact same taste in music as you, and listening to what they are buying.
algorithms.purpose: Recommends items liked by similar users.

algorithms.eli5: Because you liked a sci-fi movie with spaceships, the system recommends another movie that also has spaceships.
algorithms.purpose: Recommends items similar to past preferences based on item features.

algorithms.eli5: Compressing a massive spreadsheet of everyone's movie ratings into a few hidden 'taste' categories to predict missing ratings.
algorithms.purpose: Matrix factorization via Singular Value Decomposition.

algorithms.eli5: A student who doesn't study if they get an A, but aggressively cramming if they get a C, updating their brain one test at a time.
algorithms.purpose: Online learning updating weights only when margin/confidence is violated.

algorithms.eli5: A simple switch that flips on or off based on whether the total weight of the inputs crosses a certain threshold.
algorithms.purpose: Simplest linear neural network using a step function.

algorithms.eli5: Learning to ride a bike by taking tiny, random steps and adjusting your balance after each bump, rather than planning the whole route first.
algorithms.purpose: Optimizes linear models via mini-batch gradient descent.

algorithms.eli5: Like Random Forest, but instead of carefully choosing the best question to split a node, the tree just asks a random question, making it faster and less biased.
algorithms.purpose: Extremely Randomized Trees injecting more randomness into splits.

algorithms.eli5: A teacher who keeps giving extra homework to the students who failed the last test, until everyone passes.
algorithms.purpose: Sequentially trains weak learners, upweighting misclassified samples.

algorithms.eli5: Asking a doctor, a lawyer, and an engineer for advice, and going with the majority opinion to make a safe decision.
algorithms.purpose: Combines heterogeneous classifiers via hard or soft voting.

algorithms.eli5: Like LDA, but allowing the red team and blue team to have completely different shaped and sized clouds of players.
algorithms.purpose: Models each class with its own distinct covariance matrix.

cons: Prone to overfitting if n < m

algorithms.eli5: Like a regular SVM, but instead of tweaking a dial to control errors, you just tell it 'I want exactly 5% of the data to be support vectors'.
algorithms.purpose: Reformulation of C-SVM bounding the fraction of support vectors and errors.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a boundary line between red and blue dots, but making sure the line runs through the empty white space where there are no dots at all.
algorithms.purpose: Leverages unlabeled data by enforcing margins in low-density regions.

algorithms.eli5: Trying to draw a line through a messy scatter plot by ignoring all the crazy outliers until you find the line that fits the normal dots best.
algorithms.purpose: Iteratively fits model to inliers, robust to severe outliers.

algorithms.eli5: A line-fitting rule that treats normal errors gently, but puts a strict cap on how much crazy outliers are allowed to pull the line.
algorithms.purpose: Uses modified loss (quadratic for inliers, linear for outliers).

algorithms.eli5: Instead of drawing one single line, drawing a fuzzy cloud of possible lines, showing you where the line probably is and how unsure it is.
algorithms.purpose: Treats parameters as distributions, updating via Bayes' theorem.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a curved line (like a rainbow) through the dots instead of a straight one, by inventing new squared and cubed features.
algorithms.purpose: Extends linear regression with polynomial features for non-linear trends.

algorithms.eli5: Drawing a line that is only allowed to go up or stay flat, never going down, like tracking a plant's height over time.
algorithms.purpose: Fits piecewise constant/linear interpolating function with monotonic constraint.

algorithms.eli5: Combining the best of both worlds: throwing away useless markers (Lasso) while keeping the remaining markers from getting too big (Ridge).
algorithms.purpose: Combines L1 and L2 penalties for sparse yet stable regression.

algorithms.eli5: Filling in the blank spaces on a coloring page by guessing the color based on the average of the surrounding colors.
algorithms.purpose: Replaces missing values (NaN) using statistical measures or models.

algorithms.eli5: Assigning every word a random locker number so you don't have to keep a massive dictionary list, saving tons of memory.
algorithms.purpose: Maps categorical features to fixed-size vectors via hash functions.

algorithms.eli5: Throwing away the toys that never move or change, because they don't help you play any new games.
algorithms.purpose: Removes features with variance below a predefined threshold.

algorithms.eli5: Picking the top 10 smartest kids in the school to form a quiz team, based on their individual test scores.
algorithms.purpose: Selects top K features based on univariate statistical tests.

algorithms.eli5: Stretching or squishing all your test scores so the lowest is exactly 0 and the highest is exactly 100.
algorithms.purpose: Scales data to a fixed range, typically [0, 1].

algorithms.eli5: Figuring out if a computer can learn a rule well enough, fast enough, with high confidence, without needing to see every single possibility.
algorithms.purpose: Mathematically defines the boundaries of learnability, ensuring an algorithm can find a hypothesis with low error in polynomial time.
algorithms.outcome: A hypothesis that is approximately correct with high probability.

cons: Often overly pessimistic for practical deep learning

algorithms.eli5: Updating your belief about a coin being fair based on how it actually landed, combining your prior knowledge with new evidence.
algorithms.purpose: Estimates model parameters by maximizing the posterior distribution, incorporating prior beliefs (priors) and the likelihood of the data.
algorithms.outcome: Parameter estimates that balance data fit and prior assumptions.

algorithms.eli5: Finding the exact settings that make your current observations most likely to happen, without guessing beforehand.
algorithms.purpose: Estimates parameters by finding the values that maximize the likelihood function, making the observed data most probable.
algorithms.outcome: Parameter estimates that maximize the probability of the observed data.

cons: Prone to overfitting on small data

algorithms.eli5: Guessing the missing pieces of a puzzle, then updating your guess based on the new picture, over and over until the picture is clear.
algorithms.purpose: Iteratively finds maximum likelihood estimates for models with latent (hidden) variables by alternating between Expectation (E) and Maximization (M) steps.
algorithms.input_dataset: Data with hidden/missing variables (e.g., GMMs, HMMs).
algorithms.outcome: Converged parameters for the latent variable model.

pros: Guaranteed to converge to a local optimum

algorithms.eli5: Compressing data into the shortest possible computer file; the best theory is the one that summarizes the data most efficiently.
algorithms.purpose: Selects the model that minimizes the combined length of the model description and the data encoded using that model.

cons: Computationally hard to calculate exact description lengths

algorithms.eli5: Testing a student by giving them 10 different practice exams, each time hiding a different chapter, to ensure they really know the whole subject.
algorithms.purpose: Assesses model generalization by partitioning data into K subsets, training on K-1, and validating on the remaining fold, repeating K times.
algorithms.outcome: Average validation score and variance across K folds.

algorithms.eli5: Trying every single combination of settings on a combination lock to find the one that opens the door.
algorithms.purpose: Exhaustively searches through a specified subset of hyperparameters to find the combination that yields the best cross-validation score.
algorithms.outcome: Optimal hyperparameter set and the best estimator.

pros: Guaranteed to find the best in the grid

algorithms.eli5: Measuring how well a metal detector distinguishes between gold and junk, no matter what sensitivity setting you use.
algorithms.purpose: Plots True Positive Rate vs. False Positive Rate across all classification thresholds; AUC summarizes this into a single scalar.
algorithms.input_dataset: Predicted probabilities and true binary labels.
algorithms.outcome: ROC curve plot and AUC score (0.0 to 1.0).

cons: Can be overly optimistic on highly skewed data

algorithms.eli5: Checking if people at a party are standing close to their friends and far from strangers.
algorithms.purpose: Measures how similar an object is to its own cluster (cohesion) compared to other clusters (separation).
algorithms.input_dataset: Clustered data points and distance metrics.

algorithms.eli5: Measuring how tight the clusters are internally compared to how far apart they are from each other.
algorithms.purpose: Evaluates clustering quality by computing the ratio of between-cluster dispersion to within-cluster dispersion.

pros: Often correlates well with human intuition

algorithms.eli5: Adding a little noise to the data and seeing if the clustering algorithm gets confused and changes its mind.
algorithms.purpose: Assesses the robustness of a clustering algorithm by measuring the distance between clusterings of perturbed/noisy versions of the dataset.

algorithms.eli5: Checking if each cluster contains only one type of fruit (homogeneity) and if all apples are in the same basket (completeness).
algorithms.purpose: Measures clustering quality against ground truth labels. Homogeneity: each cluster contains only members of a single class. Completeness: all members of a given class are assigned to the same cluster.

algorithms.eli5: Comparing two different ways of sorting a deck of cards to see how much they actually agree, correcting for random luck.
algorithms.purpose: Measures the similarity between two data clusterings, corrected for chance. 1.0 means perfect match, 0.0 means random labeling.

algorithms.eli5: Choosing the best model by balancing how well it fits the data against how complicated it is, penalizing unnecessary complexity.
algorithms.purpose: Estimates the relative quality of statistical models by balancing goodness-of-fit (likelihood) with the number of parameters.

cons: Can overfit on small samples compared to BIC

algorithms.eli5: Like AIC, but with a stricter penalty for complexity, especially when you have a lot of data.
algorithms.purpose: Similar to AIC but with a stronger penalty for the number of parameters, derived from a Bayesian perspective.

algorithms.eli5: Dropping anchors in a lake, pulling boats to the nearest anchor, then moving the anchors to the center of the boats, repeating until they stop moving.
algorithms.purpose: The iterative heuristic used to solve the K-Means clustering problem by alternating between assignment and update steps.
algorithms.outcome: Local optimum of the K-Means objective function.

algorithms.eli5: Picking the first campsite randomly, but choosing the next ones as far away from existing campsites as possible to cover the whole forest.
algorithms.purpose: Smart seeding algorithm for K-Means that selects initial centroids to be spread out, drastically improving convergence speed and final accuracy.

cons: Slightly higher initialization cost than random

algorithms.eli5: Cutting a network of friends into groups so that the connections inside groups are strong, and the friendships between groups are weak.
algorithms.purpose: Partitions a graph into disjoint sets by minimizing the cost of edges cut, normalized by the total connectivity of the sets.

algorithms.eli5: Mapping a neighborhood by looking at who is connected to whom, then using the math of the map to find natural boundaries.
algorithms.purpose: Computes the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian matrix to embed data into a lower-dimensional space where clusters are linearly separable.

algorithms.eli5: Building a family tree of data points, grouping them into tiny sub-families first to save memory.
algorithms.purpose: The core data structure of BIRCH that incrementally compresses streaming data into sub-clusters (CF entries) for massive datasets.

algorithms.eli5: Organizing a library by repeatedly splitting books in half by color, then by size, so you can find any book super fast.
algorithms.purpose: Binary tree data structure for organizing points in K-dimensional space, enabling rapid nearest-neighbor searches.
algorithms.outcome: Tree structure for O(log N) spatial queries.

algorithms.eli5: Nesting smaller and smaller spheres of data inside each other to quickly find nearby points in high dimensions.
algorithms.purpose: Hierarchical data structure that partitions data using hyperspheres (balls) instead of hyperplanes, overcoming KD-Tree limitations in high dimensions.

algorithms.eli5: Blaming the neurons at the end of the line first for a mistake, and passing the blame backward so everyone learns how to do better next time.
algorithms.purpose: Computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight by applying the chain rule backwards from the output layer.

algorithms.eli5: Learning to ride a bike by taking tiny, random steps and adjusting your balance after each bump, rather than calculating the perfect path first.
algorithms.purpose: Updates model parameters using the gradient of the loss function computed on a single sample or a small mini-batch.

algorithms.eli5: A smart hiker who adjusts their step size based on the steepness of the hill and their recent momentum, so they don't overshoot the valley.
algorithms.purpose: Adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm that computes individual learning rates for different parameters using estimates of first and second moments of the gradients.
usecase_scenarios: Default optimizer for most deep learning tasks

cons: May not converge to global optimum

algorithms.eli5: Keeping a running average of how steep the hill has been recently, so you don't take too big a step on a sudden cliff.
algorithms.purpose: Adjusts learning rates by dividing the gradient by a running average of the magnitudes of recent gradients.

cons: Requires manual tuning of decay rate

algorithms.eli5: Turning a list of raw scores into a percentage chance that adds up to exactly 100%.
algorithms.purpose: Converts a vector of real numbers into a probability distribution where all outputs are positive and sum to 1.
algorithms.input_dataset: Raw logits from a neural network.

cons: Sensitive to extreme outliers (requires temperature scaling)

algorithms.eli5: Squishing any number into a probability between 0 and 1, like a decision-making funnel.
algorithms.purpose: Maps any real-valued number to the (0, 1) interval, used for binary probability outputs and gating mechanisms.

algorithms.eli5: A simple gate that blocks negative numbers but lets positive numbers pass through unchanged.
algorithms.purpose: Applies the function f(x) = max(0, x), introducing non-linearity while mitigating the vanishing gradient problem.
usecase_scenarios: Standard hidden layer activation for CNNs/MLPs

cons: Dying ReLU problem (negative values stuck at 0)

algorithms.eli5: A penalty that only cares if you are wrong or barely right; it doesn't reward you for being 'extra' right.
algorithms.purpose: Loss function used for training classifiers (like SVMs) that maximizes the margin between classes. Zero loss if correctly classified with margin > 1.

algorithms.eli5: Measuring the surprise or shock when your predicted probabilities don't match the actual reality.
algorithms.purpose: Measures the performance of a classification model whose output is a probability value between 0 and 1. Penalty increases as predicted probability diverges from actual label.
algorithms.input_dataset: Predicted probabilities and true one-hot labels.

cons: Highly sensitive to confident wrong predictions

algorithms.eli5: A penalty that treats normal errors gently, but puts a strict cap on how much crazy outliers are allowed to pull the line.
algorithms.purpose: Combines MSE and MAE. Quadratic for small errors (inliers) and linear for large errors (outliers), making it robust to outliers.

algorithms.eli5: A tolerance tube where small prediction errors are completely ignored and not penalized.
algorithms.purpose: Loss function for Support Vector Regression (SVR) that ignores errors within a certain distance (epsilon) from the true value.

algorithms.eli5: Randomly turning off some neurons during training so the network doesn't rely too heavily on any single one.
algorithms.purpose: Randomly sets a fraction of input units to 0 at each update during training time, preventing co-adaptation and overfitting.

algorithms.eli5: Resetting the scale of a seesaw after every group of kids plays on it, so it never gets stuck tilted to one side.
algorithms.purpose: Normalizes the inputs of each layer to have zero mean and unit variance, mitigating internal covariate shift.

cons: Behavior differs in train vs eval

algorithms.eli5: Looking at a 2x2 grid of pixels and only keeping the brightest one to shrink the image.
algorithms.purpose: Downsamples the input by taking the maximum value in each window, reducing dimensionality and providing translation invariance.

algorithms.eli5: Looking at a 2x2 grid of pixels and keeping their average color to shrink the image.
algorithms.purpose: Downsamples the input by taking the average value in each window, smoothing the feature map.
usecase_scenarios: Global Average Pooling for final layers

cons: Less effective at preserving sharp edges than Max Pooling

algorithms.eli5: Adding a border of zeros around an image so the edges don't get shrunk when applying a filter.

algorithms.purpose: Algorithm that learns latent representations for vertices in a network by treating short random walks as 'sentences' and applying the Skip-Gram model.

cons: Random walks may miss global structure
Does not handle node features natively

algorithms.eli5: Compressing a whole social network into a tiny summary, then trying to rebuild the original network from that summary to ensure no important friendships were forgotten.
algorithms.purpose: Unsupervised learning framework for graphs that uses a GNN encoder to map nodes to a latent space and a decoder (e.g., inner product) to reconstruct the graph adjacency matrix.
algorithms.input_dataset: Graph adjacency matrix and optional node features.
algorithms.outcome: Latent node embeddings and reconstructed adjacency matrix.

cons: Struggles with very large graphs (dense reconstruction)

algorithms.eli5: An agent that learns to get the highest score in a game, but is also rewarded for trying out new, random moves so it doesn't get stuck in a boring, suboptimal routine.
algorithms.purpose: Off-policy maximum entropy deep reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes a stochastic policy by maximizing both expected reward and policy entropy (exploration).
algorithms.input_dataset: Environment states, actions, rewards (continuous action spaces).
algorithms.outcome: Optimal stochastic policy and value functions.

algorithms.elic5: Like Q-learning, but for games where you can turn a steering wheel smoothly instead of just pressing 'left' or 'right', using two brains to guess the best smooth move.
algorithms.purpose: Off-policy actor-critic algorithm designed for continuous action spaces, combining Q-learning ideas with deterministic policy gradients.
algorithms.outcome: Deterministic policy mapping states to continuous actions.

algorithms.eli5: Training an AI by making sure it never changes its strategy too drastically in a single step, so it doesn't accidentally forget everything it just learned.
algorithms.purpose: On-policy reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes a surrogate objective function subject to a constraint on the KL divergence between old and new policies.

algorithms.eli5: Taking the basic Q-learning algorithm and combining six different proven upgrades into one super-powered AI that plays Atari games perfectly.
algorithms.purpose: Combination of six distinct improvements to the DQN algorithm: Double Q-learning, Prioritized Experience Replay, Dueling Networks, Multi-step Learning, Distributional RL, and Noisy Networks.
algorithms.input_dataset: High-dimensional states (e.g., pixels), discrete actions, rewards.
algorithms.outcome: Distribution over Q-values for each action.

cons: Computationally heavy due to distributional output

algorithms.eli5: A manager AI that sets a high-level goal ('make coffee'), and a worker AI that figures out the low-level steps ('walk to kitchen', 'grab cup', 'pour water').
algorithms.purpose: RL framework that decomposes complex tasks into a hierarchy of sub-tasks, with higher-level policies selecting goals for lower-level policies.

algorithms.eli5: A smarter version of the Adam optimizer that correctly separates the step of 'decaying weights to prevent overfitting' from the step of 'calculating the gradient update'.
algorithms.purpose: Variant of Adam that decouples weight decay from the gradient update, providing better generalization, especially for Transformer models.

algorithms.eli5: An optimizer that gives a huge learning boost to features that rarely appear, while slowing down the learning for features that appear all the time.
algorithms.purpose: Adaptive learning rate method that scales the learning rate inversely proportional to the square root of the sum of all historical squared gradients.

pros: No need to manually tune learning rate per feature
cons: Learning rate monotonically decreases, often stopping learning too early

algorithms.eli5: Like AdaGrad, but it forgets the distant past, so it only adjusts the learning rate based on how steep the hill has been recently.
algorithms.purpose: Adaptive learning rate method that divides the learning rate by an exponentially decaying average of squared gradients, solving AdaGrad's aggressive decay.

cons: Still requires manual learning rate tuning
Can be sensitive to the decay rate

algorithms.eli5: A hiker who looks ahead to see where the momentum is taking them before deciding how hard to step, preventing them from overshooting the valley.
algorithms.purpose: Variant of momentum-based gradient descent that computes the gradient not at the current weights, but at the approximate future position of the weights.

cons: Requires two gradient computations per step
Less beneficial for highly stochastic mini-batches

algorithms.eli5: A smart optimizer that remembers the curvature of the last few steps to guess the shape of the valley, making huge, accurate leaps to the bottom.
algorithms.purpose: Limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm, a quasi-Newton method that approximates the BFGS algorithm using a limited amount of computer memory.

pros: Extremely fast convergence for small problems
cons: Does not scale to large datasets (requires full-batch gradients)

algorithms.eli5: Sorting fruits into baskets, but allowing a fruit that is half-apple, half-pear to be placed 60% in the apple basket and 40% in the pear basket.
algorithms.purpose: Soft clustering algorithm where each data point belongs to every cluster with a certain degree of membership, minimizing intra-cluster variance.
algorithms.outcome: Cluster centers and fuzzy membership matrix.

algorithms.eli5: Like DBSCAN, but it automatically figures out the right 'crowd density' for different parts of a party, finding both tight groups and loose crowds without you guessing the radius.
algorithms.purpose: Clustering algorithm that extends DBSCAN by converting it into a hierarchical clustering algorithm, and then extracting a flat clustering based on cluster stability.
algorithms.outcome: Cluster labels and outlier labels (-1), plus cluster hierarchy.

cons: Can be slow on very large datasets

algorithms.eli5: A grid of neurons that physically rearranges itself so that similar inputs activate neurons that are right next to each other on the grid.
algorithms.purpose: Unsupervised neural network that produces a low-dimensional (typically 2D), discretized representation of the input space, preserving topological properties.
algorithms.outcome: 2D grid of weight vectors (map) and Best Matching Unit (BMU) assignments.

cons: Requires careful tuning of learning rate decay

algorithms.eli5: Taking a list of distances between cities and drawing a map that perfectly matches those distances, even if you don't know the actual coordinates.
algorithms.purpose: Technique that translates pairwise dissimilarities/distances between objects into a configuration of points mapped into a low-dimensional Euclidean space.
algorithms.outcome: Low-dimensional coordinate representation of data points.

cons: Sensitive to outliers in distance matrix

algorithms.eli5: Finding the hidden connection between two different sets of data, like figuring out which combination of test scores best predicts a combination of job performance metrics.
algorithms.purpose: Finds linear combinations of variables in two datasets that are maximally correlated with each other.
algorithms.input_dataset: Two multivariate datasets (X and Y) measured on the same samples.
algorithms.outcome: Pairs of canonical variates (projections) and correlation coefficients.

algorithms.eli5: Like PCA, but instead of just finding the directions with the most variance, it finds the directions that best predict the target variable you actually care about.
algorithms.purpose: Projects both predictor and response variables into a new space, finding a linear regression model by maximizing the covariance between the projected predictors and responses.
algorithms.input_dataset: High-dimensional, highly collinear predictor matrix X and response matrix Y.
usecase_scenarios: Predictive modeling with more features than samples

cons: Components can be hard to interpret

algorithms.eli5: Flattening a crumpled piece of paper in a way that ensures dots that were close together on the crumpled ball stay close together on the flat sheet.
algorithms.purpose: Linear dimensionality reduction method that finds a projection preserving the local neighborhood structure of the data, serving as a linear approximation to Laplacian Eigenmaps.
algorithms.input_dataset: High-dimensional data lying on a non-linear manifold.
algorithms.outcome: Low-dimensional linear projection matrix and embedded data.

pros: Provides explicit mapping for new data (unlike t-SNE)
cons: Sensitive to the choice of 'k' neighbors

algorithms.eli5: Using a neural network to learn the complex, hidden tastes of users and items, going beyond simple matrix multiplication to find deep patterns in what people like.
algorithms.purpose: Framework that uses multi-layer perceptrons to model user-item interactions, replacing the inner product of traditional matrix factorization with a neural architecture.

algorithms.eli5: A smart formula that not only looks at individual features (like 'user is male') but also learns how pairs of features interact (like 'male' + 'likes sci-fi') to make predictions.
algorithms.purpose: General predictor that models all interactions between variables using factorized parameters, working well with sparse data.
algorithms.input_dataset: Sparse tabular data (e.g., one-hot encoded categorical features).

pros: Works exceptionally well on sparse data
cons: Only models pairwise interactions (unless extended to HOFM)

algorithms.eli5: Combining a simple, memorizing brain (Wide) that remembers exact rules with a creative, generalizing brain (Deep) that figures out new patterns, getting the best of both worlds.
algorithms.purpose: Jointly trained linear model (Wide) and deep neural network (Deep) to combine the benefits of memorization (interpretable rules) and generalization (latent feature interactions).
algorithms.input_dataset: Mixed sparse categorical and dense continuous features.

cons: Requires manual feature crossing for the 'Wide' part

algorithms.eli5: An upgrade to Factorization Machines that adds a deep neural network to automatically learn complex feature interactions, without needing a human to manually create them.
algorithms.purpose: End-to-end model that combines a Factorization Machine (for low-order feature interactions) and a Deep Neural Network (for high-order interactions) sharing the same input embeddings.

cons: Requires large datasets to train DNN effectively

algorithms.eli5: Training a team of experts where each expert is only allowed to look at a random subset of the available clues, forcing them to learn different perspectives.
algorithms.purpose: Ensemble method that constructs multiple classifiers by training each on a random subset of features (the 'subspace'), then combining their predictions.

cons: May discard important features in some base learners

algorithms.eli5: Training decision trees on data that has been randomly rotated and scrambled using PCA, making every tree see a completely different, unique perspective of the data.
algorithms.purpose: Ensemble method that applies PCA to random subsets of features for each base classifier, rotating the feature space to increase diversity and accuracy.
usecase_scenarios: When base learners are sensitive to feature rotation (e.g., Decision Trees)

pros: Higher accuracy than Random Forest in many benchmarks
cons: Only works well with continuous data

algorithms.eli5: A single, fair score for evaluating a classifier that doesn't get tricked by imbalanced data, considering all four corners of the confusion matrix equally.
algorithms.purpose: Measures the quality of binary classifications, taking into account true and false positives and negatives, regarded as a balanced measure even for imbalanced datasets.
benchmark_metrics: MCC value (1 is perfect, 0 is random, -1 is total disagreement)

cons: Less intuitive to explain to non-technical stakeholders than Accuracy

algorithms.eli5: Grading a weather forecaster by squaring the difference between their predicted chance of rain and whether it actually rained, punishing overconfident wrong guesses heavily.
algorithms.purpose: Proper scoring rule that measures the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes (0 or 1).
algorithms.input_dataset: True binary labels and predicted probabilities.

cons: Only for binary or categorical outcomes

algorithms.eli5: Checking if a clustering algorithm grouped the same pairs of items together as the 'correct' answer key, by looking at the precision and recall of pairs.
algorithms.purpose: External evaluation metric for clustering that measures the similarity between two clusterings (e.g., algorithm output vs. ground truth) based on pairs of points.
algorithms.input_dataset: True cluster labels and predicted cluster labels.

pros: Intuitive (geometric mean of precision and recall for pairs)
Not inflated by large number of clusters
cons: Computationally heavy for very large datasets

algorithms.eli5: Scoring a clustering by checking how tight each group is, and how far apart the groups are from each other, where a lower score means better, well-separated clusters.
algorithms.purpose: Internal evaluation metric for clustering that computes the average similarity measure of each cluster with its most similar cluster, where similarity is a ratio of within-cluster distances to between-cluster distances.
algorithms.input_dataset: Feature matrix and predicted cluster labels.
algorithms.outcome: Score where lower values indicate better clustering (0 is the minimum).

cons: Only uses centroid distances, ignoring cluster shape

algorithms.eli5: Replacing a category name (like 'New York') with the average target value (like average house price) for that category, so the model instantly knows its typical value.
algorithms.purpose: Encoding technique for high-cardinality categorical features that replaces each category with the mean of the target variable for that category.
algorithms.input_dataset: Categorical features and continuous/binary target variable.
usecase_scenarios: High-cardinality categorical data (e.g., zip codes, user IDs)

algorithms.eli5: Scoring each category based on how much it 'weighs' the odds toward the positive class versus the negative class, commonly used in credit scoring.
algorithms.purpose: Encoding method that transforms a categorical variable into a continuous variable by calculating the natural log of the ratio of the percentage of non-events to the percentage of events.
algorithms.input_dataset: Categorical features and binary target variable.

cons: Can be unstable for categories with very few samples

algorithms.eli5: Filling in a crossword puzzle by using the answers you already have to guess the missing letters, then refining those guesses over several rounds until they all make sense together.
algorithms.purpose: Advanced imputation method that models each feature with missing values as a function of other features, iteratively updating imputations to converge on a consistent dataset.
algorithms.input_dataset: Tabular data with missing values (MAR or MCAR).
usecase_scenarios: Statistical analysis requiring valid standard errors
algorithms.outcome: Multiple fully imputed datasets (or a single converged dataset).

cons: Assumes data is Missing At Random (MAR)

algorithms.eli5: Instead of predicting the average outcome, it predicts the outcome for specific percentiles, like the 90th percentile (top 10%) or the 10th percentile (bottom 10%).
algorithms.purpose: Estimates the conditional quantiles of a response variable, providing a more complete picture of the relationship between variables than mean regression.
algorithms.input_dataset: Tabular data with continuous target, especially with heteroscedasticity or non-normal errors.

algorithms.eli5: Predicting the future by drawing a smooth, wiggly line through known points, while also showing a 'confidence bubble' around the line that gets wider where there's no data.
algorithms.purpose: A non-parametric, Bayesian approach to regression that provides predictions with associated uncertainty estimates by defining a distribution over functions.
algorithms.input_dataset: Small to medium tabular data where uncertainty quantification is critical.
algorithms.outcome: Predictive mean and predictive variance for each test point.

cons: Does not scale well to large datasets (O(n^3))

algorithms.eli5: Predicting how many times an event will happen (like car accidents or website clicks) based on other factors, knowing the answer can only be 0, 1, 2, 3...
algorithms.purpose: Models the relationship between a set of predictors and a count-based response variable, assuming the response follows a Poisson distribution.
algorithms.input_dataset: Tabular data with non-negative integer count targets.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m^2) via Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS)
cons: Assumes mean equals variance (often violated, requiring Negative Binomial)

algorithms.eli5: Figuring out how different factors (like age or treatment) speed up or slow down the time until a specific event happens, like a machine breaking down.
algorithms.purpose: Investigates the association between the survival time of subjects and one or more predictor variables, without assuming a specific baseline hazard distribution.
algorithms.input_dataset: Tabular data with time-to-event and censoring indicator (1=event, 0=censored).
algorithms.outcome: Hazard ratios for each feature and survival probability curves.

pros: No need to specify baseline hazard
cons: Assumes proportional hazards (effects are constant over time)

algorithms.eli5: Squishing data onto a line in a way that pushes the different groups as far apart as possible while keeping each group tightly packed together.
algorithms.purpose: Finds a linear combination of features that maximizes the separation between two or more classes (maximizes between-class variance relative to within-class variance).
algorithms.input_dataset: Continuous tabular data with class labels.
algorithms.outcome: Projected low-dimensional data and class separation boundaries.

pros: Optimal for Gaussian classes with shared covariance
cons: Fails if classes have different covariances
Requires n > m for stable covariance inversion

algorithms.eli5: Predicting a ranked outcome, like a movie rating from 1 to 5 stars, where 5 is better than 4, but the 'distance' between them isn't necessarily the same.
algorithms.purpose: Models the relationship between predictors and an ordinal dependent variable (categories with a natural order but unknown intervals).
algorithms.input_dataset: Tabular data with ordinal categorical targets (e.g., Low, Medium, High).

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m^2 * K) where K is number of categories
pros: Respects the natural ordering of categories
More powerful than treating as nominal

algorithms.eli5: Like regular logistic regression, but for guessing which of three or more unordered categories something belongs to, like predicting if a fruit is an apple, banana, or orange.
algorithms.purpose: Generalizes logistic regression to multiclass problems by modeling the log-odds of each class relative to a baseline class using a softmax function.
algorithms.input_dataset: Tabular data with nominal categorical targets (>2 classes).

algorithms.eli5: Labeling a sentence by looking at the whole sentence at once, so you know 'New' and 'York' should be grouped together as a city, not labeled separately.
algorithms.purpose: A discriminative probabilistic model for labeling and segmenting structured data (like sequences), considering the entire context of neighboring labels.
algorithms.input_dataset: Sequential data with features and target labels.
algorithms.outcome: Optimal sequence of labels for the input sequence.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m^2 * L) where L is sequence length
pros: Avoids label bias problem of HMMs
cons: Requires hand-crafted features in traditional CRFs

algorithms.eli5: Guessing the hidden weather (sunny/rainy) based only on observing what your friend is doing (walking with an umbrella or sunglasses).
algorithms.purpose: A statistical Markov model with unobserved (hidden) states, where observations are generated by these hidden states according to emission probabilities.
algorithms.outcome: Most likely sequence of hidden states (Viterbi) or state probabilities.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * K^2 * L) via Forward-Backward algorithm
cons: Markov assumption (memoryless) is often too restrictive

algorithms.eli5: Predicting tomorrow's value by looking at today's value, yesterday's value, and the average of recent prediction mistakes.
algorithms.purpose: Models and forecasts stationary time-series data using autoregression (past values), differencing (to make it stationary), and moving average (past forecast errors).
algorithms.outcome: Future time-series predictions with confidence intervals.

algorithms.eli5: Predicting the weather by looking at today, yesterday, and exactly this day last year to catch repeating seasonal patterns.
algorithms.purpose: Extends ARIMA by adding support for seasonal components (periodic patterns) in time-series data.
algorithms.input_dataset: Univariate time-series data with clear seasonality.
algorithms.outcome: Future time-series predictions with seasonal adjustments.

algorithms.eli5: Predicting how a group of friends influence each other's moods over time, rather than looking at just one person.
algorithms.purpose: Captures the linear interdependencies among multiple time series, where each variable is a linear function of past lags of itself and past lags of the other variables.
algorithms.outcome: Multivariate future predictions and impulse response functions.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * k^2 * m^2) where k is lags, m is variables
cons: Curse of dimensionality with many variables

algorithms.eli5: Predicting not just tomorrow's temperature, but how wildly it might swing up and down based on how crazy the weather has been lately.
algorithms.purpose: Models and forecasts the variance (volatility) of a time series, assuming that variance clusters over time (periods of high volatility follow high volatility).

algorithms.eli5: Predicting next year's ice cream sales by looking at last year's sales, plus knowing summer is hot and December has holidays, all automatically.
algorithms.purpose: An additive model that decomposes time series into trend, seasonality (yearly, weekly, daily), and holiday effects, robust to missing data and outliers.
algorithms.input_dataset: Time-series data with timestamps and values.
algorithms.outcome: Future time-series predictions with uncertainty intervals.

pros: Handles missing data and outliers well
cons: Less accurate than deep learning for massive data

algorithms.eli5: Matching two songs that are played at slightly different speeds by stretching or compressing the timeline to make the beats align perfectly.
algorithms.purpose: Measures similarity between two temporal sequences that may vary in speed or length by finding the optimal non-linear alignment.
algorithms.outcome: Optimal alignment path and similarity distance metric.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(N * M) or O(N) with approximations
pros: Robust to time shifts and warping
cons: Not a true metric (violates triangle inequality)

algorithms.eli5: Moving all the marbles on a bumpy table uphill until they all settle into the highest peaks, forming natural groups without you having to guess how many peaks there are.
algorithms.purpose: Non-parametric clustering algorithm that assigns data points to clusters by iteratively shifting points towards the mode (highest density region) of the data distribution.
algorithms.input_dataset: Continuous data with distinct density modes.
usecase_scenarios: When number of clusters is unknown

pros: No need to specify number of clusters
cons: Bandwidth parameter is critical and hard to tune

algorithms.eli5: A classroom voting for class representatives, where students pass messages about who they think is best, until a consensus is reached without a teacher telling them how many reps to pick.
algorithms.purpose: Clustering algorithm that identifies exemplars (representative data points) by passing real-valued messages between data points until a high-quality set of exemplars and clusters emerges.
algorithms.input_dataset: Data where a similarity matrix can be defined.
usecase_scenarios: When number of clusters is unknown

pros: No need to specify number of clusters

algorithms.algorithm_name: OPTICS (Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure)
algorithms.eli5: Like DBSCAN, but it creates a special topographic map showing the density of crowds at a party, so you can find groups of any size without guessing the exact radius.
algorithms.purpose: Density-based clustering algorithm that creates an augmented cluster ordering that captures the density-based clustering structure of the data at multiple distance thresholds.

pros: Handles varying densities better than DBSCAN
Does not require precise eps parameter

algorithms.eli5: Sorting fruits into baskets, but allowing a fruit that is half-apple, half-pear to be placed 60% in the apple basket and 40% in the pear basket.
algorithms.purpose: Soft clustering algorithm where each data point belongs to every cluster with a certain degree of membership, minimizing intra-cluster variance.
algorithms.outcome: Cluster centers and fuzzy membership matrix.

algorithms.eli5: Starting with everyone in one giant group, then repeatedly splitting the most mixed-up group in half until everyone is in their own perfect little group.
algorithms.purpose: A top-down hierarchical clustering approach that starts with all samples in one cluster and recursively splits them based on dissimilarity.
algorithms.outcome: Dendrogram and cluster labels based on a cut-off.

pros: Good at identifying large clusters early

algorithms.eli5: Asking a doctor, a lawyer, and an engineer for their opinions, then having a wise judge listen to all three and make the final, best decision.
algorithms.purpose: Combines multiple base models by training a meta-model (blender) on the out-of-fold predictions of the base models to learn how to best combine them.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(K * n * m) where K is number of base models
pros: Learns optimal weighting of base models
cons: High risk of overfitting if not careful with CV

algorithms.eli5: Like stacking, but instead of a wise judge, you just take a simple average or weighted average of everyone's answers to be safe and fast.
algorithms.purpose: A simpler variant of stacking where base models are trained on a training set, and the meta-model is trained on a separate hold-out validation set.
usecase_scenarios: When computational resources for full CV stacking are limited

cons: Uses less data for training the meta-model
Slightly lower performance ceiling than stacking

algorithms.eli5: Training decision trees on data that has been randomly rotated and scrambled using PCA, making every tree see a completely different, unique perspective of the data.
algorithms.purpose: Ensemble method that applies PCA to random subsets of features for each base classifier, rotating the feature space to increase diversity and accuracy.
usecase_scenarios: When base learners are sensitive to feature rotation

pros: Higher accuracy than Random Forest in many benchmarks
cons: Only works well with continuous data

algorithms.purpose: Ensemble method that constructs multiple classifiers by training each on a random subset of features (the 'subspace'), then combining their predictions.

cons: May discard important features in some base learners

algorithms.eli5: Learning to draw a cat by squishing it into a simple sketch, then using the sketch to draw the cat back as perfectly as possible.
algorithms.purpose: Neural network trained to copy its input to its output through a narrow 'bottleneck' hidden layer, forcing it to learn a compressed, meaningful representation of the data.
algorithms.outcome: Latent space representation and reconstructed input.

cons: Can memorize data if not regularized
Latent space can be hard to interpret

algorithms.eli5: Learning to draw a cat by squishing it into a simple sketch, then using the sketch to draw a brand new, slightly different cat that still looks real.
algorithms.purpose: Generative model that learns a probabilistic mapping between the input data and a latent space, allowing for the generation of new, similar data samples.
algorithms.input_dataset: Unlabeled data for generation (images, text, audio).
algorithms.outcome: Parameters of the latent distribution and generated samples.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m * h) per epoch + KL divergence calc
cons: Generated outputs can be blurry compared to GANs
Harder to train than standard autoencoders

algorithms.eli5: Learning to recognize a face by looking at a blurry, noisy photo and trying to reconstruct the clean, original face.
algorithms.purpose: An autoencoder trained to reconstruct the original, clean input from a corrupted (noisy) version of the input, forcing it to learn robust features.
algorithms.input_dataset: Clean data (targets) and artificially corrupted data (inputs).
algorithms.outcome: Denoised output and robust latent representations.

cons: Can be sensitive to noise type

algorithms.eli5: An art forger trying to paint a fake Mona Lisa, while a detective tries to catch the fake, until the forgery is so perfect the detective can't tell the difference.
algorithms.purpose: Framework where two neural networks (Generator and Discriminator) contest with each other in a zero-sum game to generate highly realistic synthetic data.
algorithms.outcome: Synthetic data indistinguishable from real data.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m * h) per epoch for two networks
pros: No need for explicit density functions
cons: Notoriously difficult to train (mode collapse, vanishing gradients)

algorithms.eli5: Building a super-tall Lego tower, but adding secret skip-doors so you can jump up 10 floors at once without the tower collapsing.
algorithms.purpose: Deep convolutional neural network that uses 'skip connections' or 'shortcuts' to jump over some layers, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem in very deep networks.
algorithms.outcome: Class probabilities or high-level feature maps.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m * k^2 * c * L) where L is depth
pros: Enables training of extremely deep networks
cons: Computationally heavy for very deep variants
Can still overfit on small datasets

algorithms.eli5: Glancing at a messy room and instantly pointing out where the shoes, books, and keys are all at the same time, instead of searching piece by piece.

algorithms.outcome: Bounding boxes, class labels, and confidence scores.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * m * k^2 * c) (single forward pass)
pros: Considers global context of the image
cons: Struggles with small, densely packed objects
Less accurate than two-stage detectors on complex scenes

algorithms.eli5: Tracing a picture, then zooming out to see the whole page, ensuring every single pixel is colored in perfectly with the right label.
algorithms.purpose: Convolutional network architecture with a U-shaped encoder-decoder structure and skip connections, designed for precise pixel-wise image segmentation.
algorithms.input_dataset: Medical images, satellite imagery, biological microscopy.

pros: Works well with very few training images
Precise localization due to skip connections

algorithms.eli5: Chopping a picture into tiny puzzle pieces and treating them like words in a sentence to understand the whole image.
algorithms.purpose: Applies the standard Transformer architecture directly to sequences of image patches, bypassing convolutions entirely for image classification.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(n * p^2 * d^2) where p is patches, d is dim
pros: Scales incredibly well with data and model size
cons: Requires massive datasets to outperform CNNs
Lacks the inductive biases (translation invariance) of CNNs

algorithms.eli5: Figuring out what a person is like by looking at their friends, and what their friends are like by looking at their friends.
algorithms.purpose: Neural network that operates directly on graphs, aggregating feature information from a node's local neighborhood to learn node representations.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(|E| * d) where E is edges, d is feature dim
cons: Struggles with heterophilic graphs (where neighbors are different)

algorithms.eli5: Like GCN, but instead of treating all friends equally, it learns to pay more attention to the friends who give the most useful advice.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(|E| * d * h) where h is heads
pros: Handles graphs with varying node degrees well
cons: Can over-smooth in very deep architectures

algorithms.input_dataset: Large, dynamic, or inductive graph data.

metadata.computational_complexity: O(K * |V| * d) where K is layers
pros: Scales to massive graphs via neighborhood sampling
cons: May lose some global structural information compared to full-batch GCNs

algorithms.eli5: Taking random walks through a social network and then using those walks to learn which people tend to hang out in similar circles.
algorithms.purpose: Algorithm for learning continuous feature representations for nodes in networks by optimizing a neighborhood-preserving objective using biased random walks.

pros: Captures both homophily and structural equivalence
cons: Transductive (cannot easily handle new nodes without retraining)
Random walks can be computationally expensive

algorithms.eli5: A maze runner getting a cookie for right turns and a timeout for wrong turns until it memorizes the perfect path in a cheat sheet.
algorithms.purpose: Model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the value of an action in a particular state (Q-value) to find the optimal action-selection policy.

pros: Guaranteed to converge for finite MDPs
cons: Curse of dimensionality (Q-table explodes for large state spaces)

algorithms.eli5: Using a brain (neural network) to guess the cookie-value of every possible move in a massive video game, instead of writing it all down on paper.
